unit.title: Sikh Identity and the Articles of Faith

lesson.title: The Five Kakars: Symbols of Sikh Identity
lesson.subject: sikhi

contentBlocks.text: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh formally established the Khalsa, giving initiated Sikhs a distinct, visible identity through five articles of faith known as the Five Kakars (or 'Five Ks'). Today we'll learn what each one is and what it represents.

The Five Kakars are: Kesh (uncut hair, representing acceptance of God's creation as it naturally is), Kangha (a wooden comb, representing discipline and cleanliness), Kara (a steel bracelet, representing restraint and a reminder of one's commitment), Kachera (a specific cotton undergarment, representing self-control and readiness for action), and Kirpan (a ceremonial sword, representing the duty to defend justice and protect the vulnerable). Together, these five articles make a Sikh's commitment to their faith visible and constant, worn at all times rather than only during worship.
Each of the Five Kakars carries real meaning beyond its physical form. This week, talk with a family member about what visible identity and commitment mean to them.

objectives: Name all Five Kakars and explain, in simple terms, what each one represents
Explain why the Five Kakars were established as a visible, constant identity rather than symbols worn only during worship
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 as the context for the Five Kakars.
2. Go through each of the Five Kakars one at a time, discussing both its physical form and its symbolic meaning.
3. Discuss why the Gurus chose a visible, constant identity rather than a private one — what does that visibility represent?
4. Move to the worksheet: trace each term and its meaning.
5. Close by asking the child to explain, in their own words, why visible commitment matters to the person who wears it.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on three Kakars per sitting rather than all five at once
Ready for more: research how a family member who wears the Five Kakars experiences and explains their meaning personally
This lesson is intentionally focused on identity/articles of faith — the course's 'historical persecution and resilience' strand is a separate lesson, not blended in here
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a tracing and discussion activity — there is no right/wrong answer beyond correct tracing. Check that the child can name and explain the meaning of all five Kakars by the end.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: The Five Kakars are the foundational, universally-taught content for Grade 7 Sikh-identity study, building directly on the Grade 4 introduction to Guru Nanak's core teachings.

generationData.instructions: Trace each word, say it out loud, then write it once more on your own.
